Or a better analogy would be: if Halo: Combat Evolved had the same controls as Goldeneye 007, how would it be remembered?

Adventure was designed in the late-1970s for the Atari 2600. While Adventure is, without a doubt, dated and barely playable by today's standards, it was ahead of its time, being a top-down adventure game where you controlled a character exploring a castle, looking for keys to unlock doors while fighting dragons and bats. Adventure was revolutionary for providing the template for games such as Zelda and Ultima to follow, but there is another reason why Adventure is important. Back then, Atari did not allow developers to take credit for their games, so Warren Robinett, Adventure's creator and designer, snuck in a hidden credit for himself within the game. That is the very first "easter egg" in a game and also the first time a game developer has been acknowledged for his role in the development of a video game, even if he had to bend the rules in the process.

On the contrary, ET was rushed out the door for the 1982 holiday season. The crummy Atari Pac-Man port, believe it or not, was a success, so Atari made the fatal error of assuming that if a cheaply-designed game like the Pac-Man port could be successful, a cheaply-designed video game based on the hottest movie in theaters would be even more successful, so they made one guy quickly slap together the ET game by himself and produced more ET cartridges than Atari 2600 consoles, assuming that ET would sell like hot cakes. Unfortunately for Atari, ET ended up being perhaps the biggest disaster in video-game history. Atari, of course, lost millions of dollars in the process and, of course, buried their unsold ET cartridges in a landfill in New Mexico. The failure of ET played a role in Atari losing ground, as well as the collapse of the American video-game industry in 1983.
